news_drafts.headline: Nottingham City auditors expect to issue a disclaimer of opinion on accounts by 30 November 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Grant Thornton, Nottingham City Council's external auditor, expects to issue a disclaimer of opinion on the council's accounts by 30 November 2026, according to its progress report to the Audit Committee. A disclaimer means the auditors cannot say whether the financial statements are fairly presented. The report says the date follows the committee's meeting on 27 November 2026.

The disclaimer follows a multi-year "Regaining Assurance" programme begun after the council breached the ringfence around its housing revenue account (the separate account for its own housing stock, paid for by rents). The council delivered its draft accounts on time. The auditors say their risk assessment still factors in "historic weaknesses in the control environment" identified by independent reviews after the breach. Internal audit has done limited work on journal controls, authorisation limits and segregation of duties in 2024/25 and 2025/26. Payroll testing found three leavers for whom supporting documents were missing.

The auditors say the finance team focused on meeting the 30 June statutory deadline for publishing draft accounts and did not provide information to the agreed timetable, so interim testing was delayed. Fifteen information requests were outstanding on 15 September. Against a 100% target, 25% of papers were delivered by 5 June, 43% by 15 June and 32% by 30 June.

Two further queries are open. One concerns the nature of the council's LOBO loans (bank loans where the lender may propose a higher rate on set dates and the council may repay instead of accepting it), which the auditors say may complicate work on financial instruments. The other concerns the information behind the group audit strategy. An assessment of whether group organisations account under different frameworks has been requested but not provided, and is rated red for the 30 November deadline.

The auditors say the audit is further advanced than at the same point last year. A Regaining Assurance Strategy report went to the committee in June, and an assessment of the timeline for rebuilding assurance was sent to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and the audit appointments body PSAA at the end of July.

news_drafts.headline: Nottingham forecasts £27.3m schools high-needs deficit for 2026/27, £24.2m above recovery plan
news_drafts.lead:
Nottingham City Council is forecasting a £27.3m overspend this year on high needs, the part of school funding that pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The figure is in the first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) for the Executive Board on 22 September. It is £24.2m worse than the approved recovery plan assumed, which the paper attributes to "unforeseen and unrelenting demand increases exceeding original forecasts".

The overspend would use up the £12.1m the council has set aside for it and leave a cumulative deficit of £15.2m by 31 March 2027. The worst case is £31.3m. The service is rebasing its recovery plan. A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off a council's main balance sheet, ends on 31 March 2028. After that the accounting treatment is uncertain, and any deficit would have to be met from the General Fund, the council's main budget. Because of the provision, unallocated general reserves (the cushion for the unexpected) fall to 6% of the £419.9m net budget, or £26.4m. The council's section 151 officer, its chief finance officer, recommends a minimum of 10%, or £41.99m, and says the position will be recalibrated as the schools-funding implications become known.

Elsewhere in the report, £20.1m (94%) of £21.3m of new savings is forecast to be delivered, along with £14.9m (90%) of £16.6m carried over from earlier years. That leaves £1.2m and £1.7m respectively without robust delivery plans. Adult services is forecast to overspend by £4.1m, mainly from £6.2m on external care packages.

The capital programme, the planned spending on things that last, has risen by £49m to £282.7m, including £41.5m slipped from 2025/26. The council forecasts £38.8m will not be spent this year and will move to later years.

The council reduced its borrowing by £24.3m in the quarter, with all treasury activity within approved limits. It does not expect to borrow in 2026/27.

news_drafts.headline: Nottingham City loses financial buffer in shared services partnership
news_drafts.lead: The East Midlands Shared Services partnership, which Nottingham City Council funds with £3.2 million a year, has exhausted its financial reserves. The Joint Committee approved the removal of reserves in June 2022 when they fell below best practice levels, and the balance is now entirely depleted. The partnership, which provides services jointly with Leicestershire County Council on a 50-50 basis, previously held reserves to cover redundancy costs and unexpected operational demands. Without this cushion, any overspend in the partnership's £5.8 million annual budget must now be split equally between the two councils. Nottingham City has no contingency to absorb its share of any shortfall.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: The council is working through a formal multi-year Regaining Assurance program following the HRA ringfence breach, with oversight by MHCLG and PSAA.
findings.detail: A Regaining Assurance Strategy report was presented to the Audit Committee in June 2026, and an assessment of the timeline for rebuilding assurance was submitted to MHCLG and PSAA at the end of July. Auditors will continue to consider the nature, extent and likely timing of work required as the audit progresses. The audit is notably further progressed than at the equivalent point last year.
findings.matters: Formal involvement of MHCLG and PSAA indicates regulator oversight and a structured recovery plan, but the multi-year timeline signals that confidence in the council's financial control will not return swiftly.

findings.quote: We presented our Regaining Assurance Strategy report to the Authority's Audit Committee in June. We submitted our assessment of the likely timeline for the build back of assurance over the Authority's financial statements to MHCLG and PSAA at the end of July.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: Auditors have raised potentially significant queries on group consolidation financial information and group entities' accounting policies.
findings.detail: Auditors questioned the financial information used to set group audit strategy and have raised potentially significant queries on the data. An assessment of whether group organisations account for items under different frameworks (such as FRS 102 versus Code accounting) has not been provided despite being requested. This assessment is marked as a significant delivery risk (rating R) for the 30 November deadline.
findings.matters: If group entities are miscategorized or using inconsistent accounting policies, the consolidated financial statements could materially misstate the council's financial position.

findings.quote: We have raised some potentially significant queries on the financial information on which this was based.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: Auditors have raised a specific query about the nature and accounting of the council's LOBO loans, complicating Financial Instruments audit work.
findings.detail: A separate query has been raised regarding the council's LOBO loans during the Financial Instruments audit. The report does not disclose what specific aspect prompted the query or what the council's response was, only noting that the query 'may further complicate the work in this area'. LOBO loans carry refinancing risk; auditors may be seeking clarity on accounting treatment, call dates, or terms.
findings.matters: LOBO loans create refinancing risk if lenders exercise call options; understanding their nature, terms and call dates is material to assessing the council's borrowing costs and liquidity.
findings.quote: A separate query has been raised regarding the nature of the Authority's LOBO loans, as this may further complicate the work in this area.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: The finance team delayed delivery of audit information to prioritize meeting the 30 June statutory accounts deadline, pushing audit work back by several weeks.
findings.detail: Auditors originally planned to complete interim testing before receiving draft accounts, but the finance team did not provide required information on schedule, choosing instead to focus on the statutory deadline for publishing draft accounts. As a result interim audit work was delayed. At mid-audit, 15 information requests remained outstanding. Early performance shows only 25% of papers delivered by 5 June against a 100% target, 43% by 15 June, and 32% by 30 June.
findings.matters: Delayed audit extends the period during which lenders lack financial assurance. It also suggests structural tensions between statutory publishing requirements and audit cooperation.

findings.quote: The Authority did not provide the required information in line with the agreed timetable, as the finance team focussed their efforts on meeting the statutory deadline for publishing the draft financial statements.

findings.headline: Control environment weaknesses from the HRA ringfence breach remain unresolved, with internal audit having done limited verification work in 2024/25 and 2025/26.

Internal Audit has undertaken limited work in recent years on journal controls, authorisation limits, segregation of duties, and related areas. Audit testing has also identified 3 instances in payroll testing where supporting documentation for leavers is lacking.
findings.matters: Unresolved control weaknesses mean financial errors or irregularities could occur without detection, materially misstating the accounts.

editorial.headline: Nottingham City audit opinion disclaimed as joint venture reserves depleted
editorial.standfirst: Depleted reserves in a 50:50 partnership and governance weaknesses have left the council without financial buffer or clean audit bill.
editorial.body:
Nottingham City Council faces a compounding set of financial and governance pressures that have left it without the reserves to absorb further shocks.

The council is a 50:50 partner in East Midlands Shared Services. As of 31 March 2026, EMSS reserves were fully depleted. The council's papers presented to June's joint committee meeting state: "The balance of reserve has now been fully depleted and partners will be expected to fund any operational overspend arising in year on a 50:50 basis." This leaves Nottingham City liable for half of any cost overrun.

A month later, Grant Thornton, the council's external auditor, issued a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2025/26 accounts—a rare step indicating it cannot form a view on the reliability of the financial statements. The council's papers presented to July's corporate scrutiny committee describe the work underway: "Council works closely with the External Auditor to identify the key information and evidential requirements that the auditor will need to provide a positive non-qualified audit opinion from a standard base disclaimed opinion."

But internal audit tells a deeper story. As of 31 July, the Head of Internal Audit's annual opinion for 2025/26 provides only Moderate Assurance. The audit committee papers state: "Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas." Multiple service areas remain problematic. The papers identify Adult Social Care performance and statutory compliance as an ongoing governance issue. Children's Services and Housing Services require continued improvement. Workforce capacity and resilience are constrained.

Compounding these issues is a pay award pressure. The council budgeted 3.5%, but the employers' current offer stands at 3.2%. The EMSS papers note: "Early indications suggest this offer will be rejected, with negotiations ongoing. Consequently, there remains a risk that the final award may be higher than the provision made in the budget for 2026/27."

The combination—zero reserves, audit failure, governance weaknesses not yet embedded—leaves little room for manoeuvre if budget pressures intensify.
editorial.pull_quote: Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas
editorial.watch_next: Grant Thornton is targeting a non-qualified audit opinion by March 2028, when the council's remediation efforts must demonstrate concrete results.
